c0006: Equivalent covers per day, year-1 average: about 55 dine-in (40 seats, no patio), about 55 from take-out, pickup and pre-orders, and about 20 from delivery marketplaces. A family meal counts as 3.5 covers, and a Sunday runs about 1.6 to 1.8 times a weekday (roughly 65-70 birds on the rotisseries) (Kit estimate). Compare it with the foot traffic on your street on a Sunday at noon and a Tuesday at lunch, and with your own test pre-orders
c0008: Per cover, EXCL. sales tax and tip: plates average $12.79 (a quarter chicken with 2 sides at $13.00 for 35% of covers, a half with 2 sides at $17.50 for 15%, a family meal at $34.00 counted as 3.5 covers for 30%, and a chicken sandwich or bowl at $13.50 for 20%), plus about $1.50 of extra sides, $0.36 of dessert, $0.30 of sauces and 0.65 drinks at $3.84 (Kit estimate). Family meals with a whole chicken run $31-34 in mid-size cities (menus read in October 2026). The "Menu price incl. sales tax (calculated)" row below shows the price with your local rate applied
c0010: 365 days minus Thanksgiving, Christmas Day, New Year's Day and 2 deep-clean days for the hood and the rotisseries, rounded to 360: the restaurant is open 7 days a week and holidays open like a Sunday. It is the SAME figure for the P&L, break-even, scenarios and staffing hours
c0012: Repeat neighborhood regulars, Sunday family meals and pre-orders that become a habit in year 2. It applies to covers at the same average check; staffing does NOT rise with this percentage: it comes from the "Staffing" tab
c0014: On top of year 2. Conservative: the ceiling is set by the two rotisseries (48 birds per load each) on a Sunday before the afternoon rush and by the counter at the lunch peak
c0022: Cost of goods sold on food sales: the menu averages about 29% of menu price (family meal about 29.6%, quarter with 2 sides about 28.8%, half with 2 sides about 30.0%, chicken sandwich or bowl about 21%). A marinated bird costs about $5.99 (3.0 lb (1.4 kg) at $1.75 a lb plus marinade and 5% display shrink). Chicken prices are Kit estimates: enter your distributor's and cost every plate with the Rotisserie Chicken Yield & Costing Calculator
c0024: Weighted average of sodas, Inca Kola, house-made chicha morada, beer and wine against their menu prices: about 22%. Soft drinks cost a small share of their price, while beer and wine run higher and pull the average up. If your beer distributor lends you the cooler, get the terms in writing
c0026: Family-meal boxes, vented clamshells, foil bags, sauce cups, heated-display bags, napkins and gloves for everything that leaves the restaurant, plus take-out containers for leftovers: about 4% of sales (no supplier posts a rate: Kit estimate). Some cities and states restrict foam and single-use plastics or require utensils only on request: check your local packaging ordinances
c0028: Sales through third-party delivery marketplaces (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub) as a share of total sales. Counter orders, direct pickup, pre-orders by phone or web and party trays pay no commission and do not go here. A whole rotisserie chicken travels well, but fries and yuca fries arrive soft: do not go above this share without testing it
c0030: The example uses 25%, a Plus plan on DoorDash or Uber Eats (the Basic plan is about 15% with little visibility, Premier is 30%, and app pickup orders add 6-10%). Check your contract. If you deliver yourself, enter 0 and add the driver to the "Staffing" tab as a W-2 employee, with hired and non-owned auto insurance (check your state)
c0042: About 1,600 sq ft (149 sq m) with a Type I hood and exhaust route to the roof possible (that is the filter for the space): a kitchen with the two rotisseries in view of the street, a counter with a heated display, a dining room with 40 seats, restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and storage, in a residential or retail area of a mid-size city with easy parking for pickup, second-generation space with no key money: about $28 per sq ft a year (Kit estimate, editable). The weight of rent on sales is calculated by the workbook itself in the rent row of the "3-Year P&L"
c0046: Gas for the two rotisseries and the fryers, electricity for the walk-in, the hood and makeup air and HVAC, and water. Commercial gas rates are a Kit estimate: ask the landlord for the space's utility history and ask your utility for the rate
c0048: General liability, liquor liability (beer & wine), property coverage with equipment breakdown for the refrigeration, and workers' comp. Tell the carrier you cook with gas rotisseries and fryers: it changes the premium and the terms. Rates vary by state, so get at least two quotes
c0050: Cushion for operating costs you did not budget (small repairs, spare spits or smallwares that break, menu tests)
c0057: Nominal annual rate, not APR. The example uses 10%. Ask two lenders for a quote before you set it; the rotisseries, the walk-in and the fryers can also be financed through equipment financing or a lease: compare
c0061: Years you pay interest only before principal repayment starts. The example uses 0, because SBA 7(a) loans amortize from the start. A year of interest only can ease the build-out, the hood, the gas lines and the first months of trading: ask your lender, and check the cash slack of the first repayment year on the "Break-Even" tab
c0072: One sales tax rate for the whole example (8%: state plus local, so look up yours). In this workbook it also applies to alcohol sold to go, and it equals the on-site rate, so the two rows give the same result. There is no input credit: the workbook does not recover sales tax on purchases, so that row is 0. Some states tax food to go differently, so check yours. Utilities, equipment and services use the rate in the cell below
c0079: Build-out, Type I hood and exhaust, electrical service, plumbing, gas lines, HVAC, grease interceptor, signage and facade. A 10-year straight-line life for the model; your tax depreciation schedule may differ (MACRS, Section 179), so confirm it with your CPA
c0081: Rotisseries, heated display, fryers, walk-in and refrigeration, dish machine, furniture and POS: a 7-year straight-line life for the model; your tax depreciation schedule may differ, so confirm it with your CPA
c0087: Dining room seats: 40, with no patio. Guests who pick up a pre-order or receive their food at home do not use a seat; dine-in covers average about 55 a day, so each seat turns a little more than once a day. The bottleneck of a rotisserie chicken restaurant is not the tables: it is the rotisseries on Sunday
c0089: A new rotisserie chicken restaurant draws the curious in the first month, but Sunday family meals and pre-orders take a quarter to become a habit: Month 1 (January) bills 75% of what it will bill at four months. At 100% the ramp is removed
c0091: Four months to reach full pace: January through April, so you reach May, one of the peaks of the year, with a customer base
c0093: Two months of rent before opening: the build-out, the hood and exhaust route, the gas lines and the permits. If the lender funds the loan when build-out starts, add the interest for those months, which this workbook does not count, and remember that your repayment schedule starts at closing
c0095: Cushion on the build-out and fixtures, which is where the surprises show up (the exhaust route to the roof, the electrical service, the gas lines, the grease interceptor). A lender will not finance a remodel without one
c0098: Weighted average: dine-in, counter, pickup and pre-orders (usually with a deposit) are paid at once, and the delivery marketplaces pay out what they sell every few days (15% of sales in this example)
c0100: Payment terms with your chicken, produce, oil and beverage suppliers: what they finance for you. New accounts often start on COD, and terms are the first thing you lose if you pay late
c0117: Your state or local minimum wage as an annual full-time figure (hourly rate × 2,080 hours), if it is higher than the federal $7.25 an hour. With 0, the traffic light compares only against the federal floor
c0144: Architect, MEP and hood drawings, plan review and permit fees for the build-out, the hood and the gas lines. The beer & wine license varies widely by state in cost and timing: ask your state agency early and add your own quote; this line does not assume one
c0147: Kitchen with washable wall finish and slip-resistant floor (also around the rotisseries), restrooms (one ADA-accessible), the service counter, ceilings and acoustic treatment, plus signage and facade ($5,000), so the rotisseries can be seen from the street. Second-generation space of 1,600 sq ft (149 sq m). Kit estimate: get two bids
c0149: A Type I hood of about 14 ft (4.3 m) with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air over the two rotisseries, the two fryers and the range. Hood packages run $5,000-$28,000 and the example budgets $26,000. A charcoal rotisserie is a solid-fuel appliance (NFPA 96: its own exhaust, a spark arrester and daily ash removal), so it is a variant, not the example. No manufacturer posts a price per foot: ask your mechanical contractor for a quote with your drawings, and ask the fire marshal in writing
c0151: Electrical service and panel for the refrigeration, hood, makeup air, HVAC, dish machine and rotisserie motors, plus the gas lines. Two gas rotisseries of about 177,500 BTU together need a gas service and regulator sized for them, with a gas permit. Ask for the available electrical and gas capacity BEFORE you sign the lease: a new service from the utility can take weeks or months.
c0153: Hot and cold water in the kitchen, drains with a grease interceptor ($3,500-$7,500) and HVAC for the dining room and kitchen, installed by licensed contractors with their permits and inspections
c0155: Two gas commercial rotisseries with 8 spits and 48 birds per load each. WebstaurantStore lists the Pegasus CR-8G at $6,011 retail (Oct 2026); the example budgets $13,000 for the pair with freight and installation. An electric rotisserie (Alto-Shaam AR-7E at $11,912) and a listed charcoal rotisserie (27,500 to 35,950 dollars) are variants. Size the rotisseries with your Sunday count
c0157: Heated display merchandiser that holds whole chickens at 135 °F (57 °C) or above (models run from an Avantco HDC-48 at $599 to an Alto-Shaam ED3-72 at $11,207), plus a steam table and a holding cabinet for the sides
c0159: Two 50 lb (23 kg) fryers for the yuca fries and fries (an Avantco FF50 lists at $799 and a Pitco 65C+S at $1,848) and a range with stock-pot burners for the rice & beans, the sauces and the chicha morada. Kit estimate for the range: get a quote
c0161: A 6×8 ft (1.8×2.4 m) walk-in cooler for the raw chicken and the marinade: birds marinate 24-48 hours. A Norlake Kold Locker lists at $12,808 (WebstaurantStore, Oct 2026)
c0163: Refrigerated prep table and a reach-in freezer for the frozen yuca. Raw and marinated chicken stays at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, on the bottom shelf and date-marked; the example buys birds WOG (without giblets). Kit estimate: get two quotes
c0165: 3-compartment sink, dish machine, hand sinks and a separate prep sink and stainless table for the raw chicken, kept apart from where food is served, plus shelving. Check that your spits fit the dish machine. Kit estimate
c0167: Spare spits, hotel pans, probes, scales, color-coded boards, a packing station, a sauce station (blender, squeeze bottles, portion cups), marinating tubs, the required public notices (health permit, beer & wine license, labor law posters) and allergen signs (the 9 major allergens, including sesame). Food handler cards and the CFPM exam are budgeted in the P&L
c0169: Beverage cooler and ice machine. Kit estimate. If your beverage distributor lends you the cooler, this line goes down
c0171: Tables and chairs for 40 seats in the dining room (no patio)
c0173: POS that reports sales tax, card terminal, receipt printer, online ordering for pre-orders and pickup, a counter kiosk and the tablets for the delivery marketplaces
c0178: Brand identity, a website with the menu and pre-orders, a photo shoot, a Google Business Profile and the opening campaign
c0180: Chicken, frozen yuca and fries, oil, marinade ingredients (soy sauce, aji panca, huacatay, cumin), packaging, Inca Kola, sodas, beer and wine
c0214: Rotisserie chicken (quarter, half and whole), family meals, sandwiches and bowls, and sides: about 42% dine-in, about 42% pickup and pre-orders, and about 15% through delivery marketplaces. One sales tax rate in the example, whether guests eat in or take it to go; some states tax food to go differently, so check yours
c0240: Hood and duct cleaning every quarter (NFPA 96, Table 11.4), annual service for the rotisseries and gas lines (burners, motors and spits), and the refrigeration technician. Ask your fire marshal what your jurisdiction requires
c0242: Google Business Profile, Yelp, Instagram, photos, flyers and cards with the pre-order phone and website, and the big dates: Mother's Day, Super Bowl Sunday, Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve and, if you make Peruvian pollo a la brasa, Pollo a la Brasa Day (the third Sunday of July). The opening campaign is in "Startup Costs"
c0244: POS subscription, online ordering for pre-orders, the delivery marketplace tablets, phone and internet
c0246: Cleaning supplies and degreasers, uniform and towel laundry, gloves and any lab tests or records your written food safety plan calls for
c0248: Licensed hauler for trash, cardboard, used cooking oil and the rotisserie drip-tray grease (check the pickup fee), plus annual permit renewals. Ask your city for its waste fees: this plan has not read any city fee schedule, so enter your own
c0254: CFPM certification and food handler cards, allergen training and OSHA basics for every employee: burns from the rotisseries and the fryers, cuts when carving and spitting, gas and heat
c0278: Floor for the margin after ALL variable costs (cost of goods sold, packaging, delivery marketplaces, card fees and miscellaneous). A rotisserie chicken restaurant keeps less than other concepts because the bird is most of the plate: the margin is in what goes with it. Kit estimate
c0281: Ceiling for cost of goods sold on sales: the family meal and the half chicken sit near 30% of their price, while sandwiches, bowls, sides and drinks pull the average down. If chicken prices rise, this is where you see it first. Kit estimate
c0283: Ceiling for labor on sales with an owner who is GM and head of rotisserie, a second rotisserie cook and weekend reinforcements. Kit estimate
c0287: Floor for steady-state net income so the plan holds up: 5% of sales. A well-run restaurant earns more, but this is a realistic floor, not a hope. Kit estimate
c0358: Buys the chicken and sets the bird size, makes the marinades, runs the rotisseries and the Sunday loads, handles pre-orders and manages. The workbook imputes a monthly salary as if on payroll, which is the prudent side; confirm with your CPA how you will pay yourself (owner's draw or W-2 under an S corp). The example pays the owner below a manager: owner's draw in addition from net profit
c0360: Spits and loads the rotisseries, runs the fryers and the sides, and can probe and carve. It is an investment, not an expense: if only the owner can run the rotisseries, a sick day closes your biggest day
c0362: Counter, register, phone and pre-orders, the delivery marketplace tablets and allergen information, all year round
c0364: About 16 hours a week each: the lunch and dinner rushes at the counter, packing family meals and expo. Part-time W-2 employees; tips are not modeled
c0366: Weekend help: dish, prep of the sides and sauces, and the spits through the dish machine, plus the dining room cleanup. Part-time W-2 employees
c0368: Weekend and peak-day help (Sunday, holidays and pre-order pickups): fries the yuca fries and fries and runs the line. This plan has NO delivery drivers of its own: if you add them, they are W-2 employees in most states, never independent contractors by default (check yours), and you need hired and non-owned auto insurance
c0384: Hours the restaurant is open to the public each day, 7 days a week, on average, adding the preparation for each service. Any slow stretch between services is not counted
c0386: Average number of people on at once between the rotisseries, the fryers, the counter and the packing station. On a Sunday more are needed: the weekend help and the extra counter staff come in (the annual schedule does not see this: put it on the shift schedule)
c0388: Hours of production before opening each day: spitting the marinated birds and loading the first batch, lighting the rotisseries, and prepping the sides, sauces and fry station
c0390: The owner with the rotisserie cook. Closing, cleaning the rotisseries and the hood, and purchasing are outside this schedule: they are the margin between the hours hired and the hours needed
c0406: 4. All figures are EXCL. SALES TAX. To turn a menu price into a price excl. sales tax, divide it by 1 plus your sales tax rate (a rate of 8% means dividing by 1.08). The example uses ONE rate for everything: dine-in, take-out, delivery and beverages; some states tax food to go or alcohol differently, so check yours. The P&L is excl. sales tax; the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab shows what you actually collect, sales tax included, and the sales tax you remit as a quarterly filer.
c0408: 6. The "12-Month Cash Flow" tab answers the question that decides a bank deal: in which month the cash runs out. Its Month 1 is JANUARY, in calendar order: the ramp-up falls on January and February, the slowest months, and that is why working capital counts. May, July and December are the peaks. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row. The minimum balance of the year can never show in red.
c0410: 8. The Word business plan in this pack quotes the figures in this Excel: if you change a green cell, the Excel rules. The Rotisserie Chicken Yield & Costing Calculator is separate and is used to measure the cooked yield of a bird, how many birds fit on your rotisseries before the Sunday peak, and to COST each bird and each plate: do not copy the food cost of one bird into the "0. Assumptions" tab. The "Cost of goods sold on FOOD sales" cell is the weighted average of the WHOLE menu (quarter, half, whole, family meals, sandwiches and bowls, and sides, each by what it sells) plus waste, and that is why it differs from the food cost of the whole bird. With the costing of your own menu, check that this average holds.
